17154.heading: Cayley Table
17154.content:
A Cayley table records the result of a finite binary operation with one operand labeling each row and the other labeling each column. It makes closure, identity candidates, inverses, and commutativity visible.

A completed table still requires an associativity argument before it proves that the structure is a group.

17157.title: Causal Symmetry
17157.heading: Causal Symmetry
17157.content:
A causal symmetry exists when relabeling outcomes leaves their probability distribution unchanged while the collective conditions that determine the phenomenon's causal structure remain the same. Outcomes related by that invariant structure must receive equal probabilities.

The concept provides an objective route from causal conditions to probability values. It avoids treating observed frequency alone as the source of probability.

17160.title: Causal Correlation
17160.heading: Causal Correlation
17160.content:
A causal correlation reflects a relationship in which changing one factor, under the relevant conditions, changes another. Such a relationship can support intervention and, when the conditions persist, prediction.

Not every statistical association has this status. Establishing causal meaning requires evidence about variation and structure rather than the magnitude of correlation alone.

17235.heading: Capacitor Discharging
17235.content:
A capacitor discharging through a resistor loses charge exponentially:

$$Q=Q_0e^{-t/RC}.$$

Voltage follows the same decay, while current has the corresponding magnitude and opposite charging direction. The time constant $RC$ is the time for charge or voltage to fall to $1/e$, about 37 percent, of its initial value.

17238.heading: Capacitor Charging
17238.content: In a series RC circuit connected to a constant supply, capacitor voltage rises as $V_C=V_0(1-e^{-t/RC})$ while current falls as $I=(V_0/R)e^{-t/RC}$. The time constant $RC$ sets the pace: after one time constant the capacitor has reached about 63 percent of its final charge.

17241.content: Capacitance measures how much charge a pair of conductors stores per unit potential difference: $C=Q/V$. Its SI unit is the farad. Capacitance depends on conductor geometry and the dielectric medium rather than on the instantaneous charge or voltage while the system remains linear.

Matching selected effects prevents virtual content from appearing unnaturally clean or geometrically perfect beside the captured scene. The simulated parameters must correspond to the actual camera and its current settings.

17304.heading: Camera Exposure

Forensic exposure analysis compares those visible effects with the values recorded in [[EXIF Metadata]]. Computer-vision pose estimates assume these values are known. Incorrect calibration creates systematic registration error, so the same camera configuration and image settings used during calibration must remain valid during tracking.

17370.title: C# Structs and Value Types
17370.heading: C# Structs and Value Types
17370.content:
A C# struct defines a value type. Assigning or passing it normally copies its value rather than sharing the identity of one heap object, and a struct cannot inherit from another class or struct.

Structs can still define fields, methods, properties, constructors, operators, and interfaces. They are best suited to compact values whose identity is their data. Large mutable structs can create confusing copies and unnecessary movement, so class and struct are semantic as well as memory-management choices.

17373.content:
C# tuple syntax groups several values into one lightweight result. Naming tuple elements replaces generic positional names with domain meaning, and inferred names can carry suitable local identifiers into the tuple.

Deconstruction assigns the elements into separate variables in one statement, while discards ignore values the caller does not need. Tuples suit local combinations with little behavior; a dedicated type is clearer when the group needs validation, methods, or a stable public contract.

A tuple groups values of potentially different types into one returnable result. Older `Tuple<...>` instances expose positional members such as `Item1`, while language-level tuples can name and deconstruct the returned elements more clearly.

A C# switch expression maps an input value to a result through a sequence of pattern-and-expression arms. It removes the repeated `case`, assignment, and `break` structure of a statement when the purpose of the decision is simply to produce one value.

Arms are considered in order, so specific patterns should precede broad ones. The discard pattern supplies a default result. Because the construct is an expression, it can initialize a variable directly and makes the common output of all branches visible.

A switch expression places the input before `switch` and maps patterns to results with concise arms. The discard pattern `_` supplies the fallback arm, replacing the statement form's explicit `default` label when the goal is to compute a value.

17382.heading: C# Static Constant and Readonly Fields
17382.content:
A static field is shared by all instances of a type. A constant is substituted into calling code at compile time and must be expressible as a supported literal, while a readonly field is assigned at declaration or construction and remains a live field reference.

Readonly fields are safer for public values that may change between library versions because callers observe the field after recompilation of the library. Constants are appropriate only when the value is truly permanent and known at compile time.

17388.heading: C# Recursive Functions
17388.content:
A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself with a smaller or simpler input. It requires a base case that returns without another call and a recursive case that makes progress toward that base.

Each call consumes stack space until it returns, so missing or unreachable termination can cause a stack overflow. Recursive definitions can closely match problems such as factorials, but their numeric result can still overflow the chosen return type even when the recursion itself terminates correctly.

Hiding a member creates a separate compile-time choice and is not the same as overriding it. Abstract members require derived implementations, while sealed types or members prevent further inheritance or overrides when an extension point would violate the design.

Polymorphism lets code invoke a common contract while the runtime type supplies the concrete behavior. Overriding inherited operations and implementing abstract members are dynamic forms; method or operator overloading chooses among statically known signatures.
